stem: At sunrise, Sita faces East (towards the sun). She then turns 90 degrees to her right. In which direction does her shadow now fall?

per_option_rationale.rationale: The sun is in the East so shadows always fall West at sunrise. After a right turn from East, Sita faces South. West is to the right of someone facing South.
Left of a person facing South is East, not West. Choosing left confuses the relative direction after the turn.
In front means South (the direction she faces), but shadows fall opposite to the sun; the sun is East so the shadow is West, not South.
Behind a South-facing person is North, not West; the shadow direction was not re-mapped after the turn.

explanation: At sunrise the sun is in the East, so shadows fall in the opposite direction - West. This does not change when Sita turns. After turning 90 degrees right from East, she faces South. For a person facing South, West is to their right. So the shadow falls to her right.

explanation_sections.punchline: Shadow is always West at sunrise regardless of which way Sita turns; facing South, West is to her right.
explanation_sections.approach: Deductive trace: Step 1 - fix shadow direction: sun in East means shadow always falls West. Step 2 - determine new facing: East + right 90 = South. Step 3 - orient West relative to South-facing person: facing South, left=East, right=West. Shadow is to her right.
explanation_sections.lesson: Shadow direction depends only on the sun's position, not the person's facing. After fixing the absolute shadow direction, map it to left/right/front/back relative to the new heading.
explanation_sections.timing: 45-60 seconds. The two-step trap: first establish absolute shadow direction (West), then determine relative side for the new facing (South). Mixing up left and right for a South-facing person is the key error (options 1 vs 2).
